old_caption: The video begins with a first-person perspective inside a water slide, illuminated by green lights. The camera is positioned at the rider's feet, showing the smooth, dark interior of the slide. As the ride progresses, the camera moves forward through a series of twists and turns, capturing the dynamic motion and the changing angles of the slide. The lighting remains consistently green throughout the visible sequence. The camera continues to capture the smooth, curved surfaces of the slide, emphasizing the thrill and speed of the ride. The video concludes with the rider emerging into a brightly lit area, where the slide opens up to reveal a large, circular exit. The final scene shows the rider's feet as they step out onto a platform, completing the exhilarating journey down the water slide.

caption: A first-person 360-degree view places the camera low on an enclosed water slide, with the rider's feet in black water shoes visible at the bottom center of the frame. Ahead, a smooth tube glows green and cyan, its walls curving around a fork that splits into two circular openings, one bright white on the left and one vivid cyan on the right, separated by a dark central divider. The view shifts gradually through the tube, so the openings change apparent size and position and the curved walls alter their apparent extent over time. Water texture and highlights move across the slide floor between the feet and the openings, shifting continuously. A horizontal projection seam crosses the mid-frame, dividing the dark blue upper region from the illuminated tube below. The dark divider between the openings changes apparent shape and position as perspective shifts and reflections move.

endpoints are normal, not physical errors. Do not add unseen causes, onset, stopping or outcomes.
An internal editing cut is not evidence of physical motion connecting the views.

Check identification before physical interpretation: a reflection is not a separate actor;
a powder/smoke/liquid outline or shadow is not automatically the boundary of a solid object;
an apparent change caused by occlusion/viewpoint is not automatically material deformation.
Do not claim contact, bending, compression, melting, disintegration or structural recovery unless
the appropriate material/surface itself provides visible evidence. Do not infer a force or earlier
collision just because the visible configuration would be compatible with it.
Compare several frames before asserting translation, rotation, direction, unchanged position or
camera tracking. A single visible texture/seam does not prove spin. Avoid unnecessary absolute
claims of stillness, no motion, no camera motion or 'exactly' synchronized changes.
Remove invented scene details and explanations, but keep clearly visible ongoing motion and
processes. Avoid deleting the real process merely because its cause lies outside the cropped window.

draft_caption: A first-person 360-degree view places the camera low on an enclosed water slide, with the rider's feet in black water shoes anchored at the bottom center of the frame. Ahead, a translucent tube glows green and cyan, its walls curving around a fork that splits into two circular openings, one bright white on the left and one vivid cyan on the right, separated by a dark central divider. The rider travels steadily forward through the tube, so the two openings grow larger and the curved walls spread toward the frame edges as the segment progresses. Water ripples and bubbles flow across the slide floor between the feet and the openings, shifting continuously. A horizontal projection seam crosses the mid-frame, dividing the dark blue upper region from the illuminated tube below. The dark divider between the openings changes apparent shape and position as perspective shifts and reflections move. The 'Attractions 360°' watermark remains fixed at the bottom right.
